messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 30
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Software Engineer
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 46

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Gustatory (Taste): A specific taste associated with the event, Olfactory (Sweat/Body): Sweat or body odour, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Threat: Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
  Memory: Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order, Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Blocked Before Complete: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Anika Patel is a 30-year-old software engineer who came to treatment after years of trying to keep her distress contained within the routines of adult life. She is married and lives with her husband in an apartment she has worked hard to make feel orderly and secure, but the sense of safety she wants from it never quite settles in. When she speaks about her childhood, she does not offer a single clear story so much as fragments that stop and start. She was physically abused by a caregiver when she was young, and even in the first sessions she struggled to tell it in sequence. She would begin with an image of being trapped in a room at home, then lose the thread, correct herself, and go quiet. It was clear that the memories did not arrive for her as a narrative she could walk through from beginning to end. They came in pieces, and once they came she was quickly overtaken by feeling and had to stop.

What she could describe made the atmosphere of those experiences vivid. She remembers being close enough to the caregiver to smell sweat and stale alcohol on their breath and clothes. There was also a particular taste that she still associates with those moments, something so specific that she notices it immediately in the present and feels her body tense before she has fully registered why. In her account, the sensory details are more available than the order of events. She knows there were repeated episodes of being hurt, but when she tries to place one moment before another, the timeline collapses. She has come to dread the memories not only because of what happened, but because recalling them feels like standing too close to something unbearable. When a fragment returns, she becomes overwhelmed so quickly that she cuts herself off, changes the subject, or tells herself not to think about it any further.

Over time these reactions became woven into ordinary adult situations. In the office, where she works on a software team in long stretches of close collaboration, she is acutely aware of smells in a way that feels disproportionate even to her. If a coworker comes back from lunch with alcohol on their breath after a happy hour, or if she catches the sour smell of sweat in a crowded conference room after people have rushed in from outside, she feels a jolt of alarm and has to concentrate on appearing normal. She may excuse herself to the restroom, stand at the sink, and wait for the wave of emotion to pass. She does not explain this to colleagues; from the outside, it can look as though she is simply private or easily overstimulated. At home, certain foods or flavors can bring the same abrupt reaction. A taste will hit her and she is no longer just eating dinner with her husband; she is fighting the urge to push the whole memory system away before anything fuller emerges.

Sleep has become one of the clearest places where her distress shows itself. At night she has trouble falling asleep, and if she wakes she often cannot settle again. The apartment is objectively secure, and she knows this, but knowledge does not translate into ease. She checks the front door lock, then checks it again, then moves to the windows. If her husband reassures her that everything is locked, she may believe him for a moment and still feel compelled to verify it herself. She describes lying in bed with her body braced, unable to relax even when nothing is wrong. What frightens her most in those moments is not a specific expectation that someone is about to enter, but the feeling that letting down her guard would be a mistake. Her husband has grown concerned and sometimes frustrated, especially when the checking stretches late into the night and leaves them both tired the next morning.

The strain has begun to touch her work as well. On days after poor sleep, she finds it harder to focus on complex coding tasks and more difficult to tolerate the bustle of the office. She has started timing her office attendance to avoid social events where alcohol may be present, and when team gatherings happen she often leaves early with a practical excuse. She knows these choices narrow her life, but they also make sense to her: they reduce the chances of being hit by a smell or taste that will leave her flooded and struggling to regain composure.

What brought Anika to seek help now was not a new trauma, but the accumulating realization that she is organizing more and more of her life around not being caught off guard. She is exhausted by broken sleep, embarrassed by the repeated checking, and discouraged by how quickly she becomes overwhelmed whenever she tries to remember what happened to her as a child. She says she wants, more than anything, to be able to be at home with her husband and feel that she is actually there, rather than on alert. At the same time, she is afraid that if she lets herself remember more fully, the feelings will be too much to bear.
